query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a controlled minor fraction of chromium (Cr) to equal-atomic BCC NbMoTaW will improve room-temperature ductility and enhance irradiation tolerance while preserving high-temperature mechanical strength and BCC phase stability.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW that exhibits excellent strength at high temperature (up to 1600 °C) but poor room-temperature ductility and only computationally inferred irradiation resistance.
generation.intervention: Introduce approximately 5–10 atomic % Cr to form a quinary NbMoTaWCr alloy.
generation.conditions: Testing should include room-temperature mechanical deformation for ductility improvement, high-temperature (up to 1600 °C) loading conditions for mechanical strength validation, and irradiation conditions (e.g., helium implantation or heavy ion irradiation) to assess defect evolution and stability.
generation.structural_mediator: Retention of a predominantly BCC single-phase structure with minor lattice distortions induced by Cr addition; these distortions are expected to act as effective sinks for irradiation-induced defects without triggering deleterious secondary phase precipitation.
generation.mechanism: Chromium is hypothesized to enhance atomic mobility and provide additional slip systems at room temperature, thereby improving ductility. Concurrently, its introduction should increase the ability of the alloy to self-heal under irradiation by promoting defect recombination at the Cr-induced distortion sites. Careful control of the Cr content should prevent the formation of embrittling precipitates while balancing solid solution strengthening.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the NbMoTaWCr alloy is expected to exhibit a measurable increase in room-temperature ductility and improved irradiation tolerance (i.e., fewer irradiation-induced defects such as amorphization or blistering) while maintaining similar high-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.baseline: The current NbMoTaW alloy demonstrates excellent high-temperature performance but suffers from poor room-temperature ductility and lacks experimental validation of its irradiation resistance.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are anticipated when Cr content is kept in the range of ~5–10 atomic %. Testing boundaries include room temperature for ductility assessments, high temperatures up to 1600 °C for strength retention, and irradiation regimes representative of helium implantation or comparable radiation damage environments.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Cr concentration has yet to be determined, and there is uncertainty regarding whether minor Cr additions may inadvertently promote undesired precipitate formation under long-term thermal or irradiation exposure.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of NbMoTaWCr alloys with varying Cr content (e.g., 0%, 3%, 5%, 7%, 10%). Conduct room-temperature tensile tests to quantify ductility, high-temperature (up to 1600 °C) mechanical tests to measure strength retention, and controlled irradiation experiments (using helium implantation or heavy ion irradiation) to evaluate defect accumulation and structural stability. Follow these with detailed microstructural characterization (using TEM, SEM, and XRD) to detect any formation of undesired precipitates.
measurements: High-temperature mechanical strength (compression and tensile tests at 1600 °C)
Post-irradiation defect density and microstructure via TEM/SEM
Phase analysis via XRD to detect secondary precipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the NbMoTaWCr alloys either do not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility and irradiation resistance compared to the base NbMoTaW alloy, or if the addition of Cr results in the formation of deleterious secondary phases that compromise the high-temperature mechanical strength and overall stability of the BCC structure.

cited_evidence.text: W-based refractory HEAs (RHEAs) have been recently developed in the context of high-temperature applications, showing high melting temperature (above 2873 K) and superior mechanical strength at high temperatures compared to Ni-based superalloys or pure W,. Combining the two approaches above, the authors have recently developed a refractory low-activation HEA based on W-Ta-Cr-V. Its response to loop formation under ion irradiation and He implantation is enhanced compared to previously developed W-based alloys, showing no noticeable dislocation loop formation and smaller He bubbles with no radiation-induced segregation at grain boundaries upon heavy ion irradiation and He implantation, respectively. However, this quaternary RHEA demonstrated Cr- and V-rich precipitates which could be detrimental to mechanical properties in terms of embrittlement. In this study, a design strategy to further improve the overall response of the W-Ta-Cr-V RHEA is introduced and resulted in the development of a quinary RHEA with improved resistance to high-temperature and irradiation environments. AbstractRefractory metal high-entropy superalloys (RSA), which possess a nanoscale microstructure of B2 and bcc phases, have been developed to offer high temperature capabilities beyond conventional Ni-based alloys. Despite showing a number of excellent attributes, to date there has been little consideration of their microstructural stability, which is an essential feature of any material employed in high temperature service. Here, the stability of the exemplar RSA AlMo0.5NbTa0.5TiZr is studied following 1000 h exposures at 1200, 1000 and 800 °C. Crucially, the initial nanoscale cuboidal B2 + bcc microstructure was found to be unstable following the thermal exposures. Extensive intragranular precipitation of a hexagonal Al-Zr-rich intermetallic occurred at all temperatures and, where present, the bcc and B2 phases had coarsened and changed morphology. This microstructural evolution will concomitantly change both the mechanical and environmental properties and is likely to be detrimental to the in-service performance of the alloy.Keywords: refractory metal high entropy alloys, phase transformation/precipitation, intermetallics, thermodynamics
